title: Suprapubic catheter insertion
subtitle: Full bladder, no bowel in the way

sources.title: British Association of Urological Surgeons' suprapubic catheter practice guidelines (Harrison SCW et al., BJU International)
Evidence-based guidelines for best practice in urological health care: catheterisation, indwelling catheters in adults, urethral and suprapubic

indications: Acute retention where urethral catheterisation has failed or is contraindicated (suspected urethral injury, false passage, urethral stricture).
Long-term bladder drainage, where a suprapubic route is preferred to a long-term urethral catheter (urethral erosion, patient preference, sexual activity, neurogenic bladder).
Urinary diversion in Fournier gangrene or perineal trauma.
contraindications: A bladder that cannot be confidently filled and identified.
Known or suspected bladder cancer, where the tract may seed tumour.
Uncorrected coagulopathy and anticoagulation that cannot be safely managed.
Previous lower abdominal or pelvic surgery, or a pelvic mass, is a relative contraindication to blind insertion: use ultrasound guidance, cystoscopic guidance, or an open approach.
preparation: Confirm a full bladder by palpation and ultrasound; fill it through a urethral catheter or cystoscope where possible.
Ultrasound the lower abdomen to look for bowel between the skin and the bladder.
Consent covers bleeding, infection, bowel injury, catheter blockage or displacement, and long-term catheter care.
Antibiotic prophylaxis per local policy, particularly in a patient with a long-term urethral catheter or known infected urine.
positioning: Supine, with slight head-down tilt to move bowel away from the bladder; lithotomy if cystoscopic guidance is used.
equipment: Suprapubic catheter kit (trocar and sheath, or Seldinger set) and an appropriately sized catheter.
Local anaesthetic, a long seeker needle, skin suture or fixation device.
Flexible or rigid cystoscope if cystoscopic guidance is used.
anatomy: The full bladder rises out of the pelvis and pushes the peritoneal reflection upwards, leaving an extraperitoneal window above the pubic symphysis.
An empty bladder lies behind the pubis, with peritoneum and bowel above and in front of it.
The insertion site is in the midline, about two finger-breadths above the symphysis, below any lower abdominal scar.
The inferior epigastric vessels lie lateral to the midline; staying in the midline avoids them.
criticalSafety: Never insert a suprapubic catheter into a bladder that is not clearly full.
Aspirate urine with the seeker needle before inserting the trocar; no urine means stop.
Previous lower abdominal surgery: image first and use ultrasound or cystoscopic guidance, or an open approach.
structuresAtRisk: Bladder base and prostate (trocar passed too deep)
commonErrors: Inserting into a partially filled bladder.
Choosing an insertion point too high, above the peritoneal reflection, or too close to the pubis.
Pushing the trocar through the back wall of the bladder.
Inflating the balloon before urine flows freely.
complications: Bowel perforation, which can present days later as peritonitis.
Urinary infection; wound infection at the tract.
Catheter dislodgement before the tract has matured.
postop: Observe for abdominal pain, peritonism or sepsis in the first days; new abdominal signs are a bowel injury until proven otherwise.
Plan the first catheter change, which is usually done by the urology team because the tract is immature.
Give written catheter care instructions to the patient and community team.
Document catheter type, size, balloon volume, the insertion technique and any imaging used.

steps.emphasis: Infected urine is common in this group; follow culture results where available.
Slight head-down tilt helps bowel fall away from the bladder.
Where cystoscopic guidance is used, fill the bladder and watch the needle enter in the midline at the dome. Transillumination helps confirm the site.
Light pressure around the tract usually suffices; persistent bleeding needs ultrasound and a senior opinion.
Secure the catheter with a skin suture or fixation device; do not close the skin around it tightly.

step.spc.ultrasound.title: Ultrasound: full bladder and no bowel
step.spc.ultrasound.why: Bowel injury is the complication that kills after suprapubic catheterisation, and ultrasound is the cheapest way to prevent it.
how: Confirm a distended bladder in two planes.
Look for bowel loops between the anterior abdominal wall and the bladder along the planned track, especially below a scar.
Mark the site in the midline above the symphysis, and estimate the depth to the bladder.
pitfalls: Accepting a palpable mass as the bladder without imaging it.

step.spc.seeker.title: Local anaesthetic and seeker needle aspiration
step.spc.seeker.why: Aspirating urine confirms the track and depth before the large trocar goes in. No urine means the trocar must not follow.
how: Infiltrate local anaesthetic into the skin and down the planned track.
Advance a long needle perpendicular to the skin, or angled slightly towards the pelvis, aspirating as you go, until urine is aspirated.
Note the depth at which urine appears. If no urine is obtained, stop and reassess with ultrasound.
pitfalls: Multiple blind passes searching for the bladder.
Aspirating blood or faeculent material and continuing.

step.spc.insert.title: Trocar or Seldinger insertion and catheter placement
step.spc.insert.why: The track has been proven; the risk now is depth. Too shallow and the catheter sits in the abdominal wall; too deep and the trocar injures the back wall or the bladder base.
how: Make a small skin incision at the site and insert the trocar along the same track as the seeker needle, with controlled pressure and a hand stop.
Once urine flows, advance the catheter through the sheath well into the bladder, then remove the sheath per the kit design.
Inflate the balloon only after free drainage of urine, with sterile water to the specified volume.
pitfalls: Losing control of the trocar as it gives through the bladder wall.
Inflating the balloon in the abdominal wall or the prevesical space.

step.spc.secure.title: Confirm drainage and secure the catheter
step.spc.secure.why: An immature tract closes quickly if the catheter falls out, and the replacement may need a second procedure.
how: Confirm free drainage and clear or clearing urine.
Secure the catheter and apply a dressing; connect to a closed drainage system.
Leave a urethral catheter in place temporarily only if there is a specific reason, and document it.
pitfalls: A catheter secured under tension that kinks and blocks.
